draft.title: Sound as a wave
card: Sound is a vibration. A vibrating object, such as a guitar string, pushes on nearby particles and sets them vibrating.
The vibration is passed from particle to particle through a medium, which is the material the sound travels through. The particles move back and forth and do not travel with the sound.
Sound travels faster in solids than in air, because the particles in a solid are packed closer together and pass the vibration on sooner.
Sound needs particles to travel through. It cannot travel through a vacuum, which is empty space with no particles.
draft.remember: Sound is a vibration passed on by particles, so it needs a medium and is faster in solids than in air.

a.q: Why can astronauts not hear a spacecraft's engine from outside in space?
opts: Space is a vacuum, so no particles pass on the vibration
Space is too cold for sound to be made at all
Sound travels too slowly through solids to be heard
The engine's particles are too far from the astronaut
a.why: Sound needs particles to pass the vibration along. Space is mostly a vacuum with almost none, so the sound cannot travel. Cold is not the reason, since the problem is the lack of a medium.
a.clue: What does sound need to pass from one place to another?

b.q: Ari puts an ear against a long steel fence and a friend taps the far end. Ari hears the tap before the sound arrives through the air. Why?
opts: Sound travels faster in a solid than in air
Sound travels faster in air than in a solid
The tapped steel moves along the fence to Ari's ear
Sound travels through steel but not through air
b.why: The particles in steel are close together, so they pass the vibration on faster than the spread-out particles in air. The steel itself does not move along the fence. Sound does travel through air, just more slowly.
b.clue: Compare how close together the particles are in steel and in air.

a.best: Space is a vacuum, so no particles pass on the vibration

b.best: Sound travels faster in a solid than in air

problems.detail: The card says sound is faster in solids because the particles are packed closer together. This is a simplification that can mislead. The main reason is that particles in a solid are strongly bonded (the solid is stiff), so they pass the vibration on quickly. Closer packing on its own would not make sound faster. Consider wording such as 'particles are close together and strongly linked'.
Why (b) repeats the same incomplete reasoning: that steel passes the vibration on faster only because its particles are close together. It does not mention the strong bonds or stiffness in steel.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear answer each. The card and why (b) explain the faster speed of sound in solids only by close particle packing, which is an incomplete reason. They should mention strongly bonded particles (stiffness).
